newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean auto workers plan half-day strike.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean auto workers plan half-day strike.

text.p: Union workers at South Korea's two major carmakers said they would halt production for several hours on Friday to pressure parliament to speed up the revision of a controversial labour law.
Union leaders at Hyundai Motors Co and Daewoo Motors Co said they would honor a strike call by an outlawed umbrella union group, the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.

Kwon Young-kil, president of the confederation, called for the partial strikes in a news conference on Thursday, and said they could become full-blown stoppages next week if the law was not revised to their satisfaction by midnight on Friday.
An organisation representing unions at 21 Hyundai Group affiliates has also called for a half-day strike, but it was not immediately clear how many Hyundai unions would join.
"We are striking to show our unhappiness over the way the labour law is being treated in parliament," said a Hyundai Motors union official who declined to be named.

Ruling and opposition members of parliament have said they were trying to work out a joint proposal for revising the labour law, which makes its easier for companies to sack workers and replace striking employees.
The law, originally rammed through parliament on December 26, sparked more than three weeks of wildcat strikes that forced President Kim Young-sam to return it to parliament for revision.
A parliamentary committee began reviewing the law two weeks ago but has deadlocked over opposition demands for the deletion of a clause banning companies from paying striking workers.
"The deadlock seems to be over whether or not the 'no work, no pay' clause should be included," said Yoon Ho-jung, vice spokesman for the opposition National Congress for New Politics.

But Yoon said his party and the ruling New Korea Party had agreed to legalise the outlawed labor confederation, and were nearing agreement on a proposal to delay for two years a clause in the law allowing companies to lay off workers.
The law is due to go into effect on March 1 but government officials have said it will not be enforced.
